interactions.label: Filter Order (N)
interactions.teaches: Controls the size of the binomial filter (N=1 is 2x2, N=2 is 3x3, N=3 is 4x4). Increasing the order makes the discrete bell shape wider and smoother, converging toward a Gaussian.

interactions.label: Show Separability
interactions.teaches: Reveals that this 2D filter is separable: it is created by multiplying a 1D vertical binomial vector by a 1D horizontal binomial vector.
Hovering over individual stems displays their exact binomial coordinate and fractional/integer weight.

demo_steps.title: The 2D Binomial Filter (N=2)
demo_steps.narration: This is the b_{2,2}[n,m] binomial filter. It forms a discrete symmetric bell shape with a central peak of 4 and outer corners of 1. It acts as a smooth, isotropic low-pass filter that avoids the ringing artifacts of a box filter.

demo_steps.title: Separable Construction
demo_steps.narration: Enable separability to see how this 2D filter is composed. The 2D grid of coefficients is the outer product of a 1D row filter [1, 2, 1] and a 1D column filter [1, 2, 1]^T. This makes 2D convolution extremely efficient because it can be computed as two successive 1D convolutions.

demo_steps.title: Minimal 2x2 Filter (N=1)
demo_steps.narration: Lowering the order to N=1 yields a simple 2x2 neighborhood. The coefficients are [1, 1] horizontally and vertically, producing a uniform flat-topped 2D filter. This is the smallest possible binomial blur.

demo_steps.title: Higher Order Blur (N=3)
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the order to N=3 produces a 4x4 grid based on the 1D binomial coefficients [1, 3, 3, 1]. The central coefficients rise to a peak of 9. As N increases, the discrete distribution rapidly approaches a perfect circular 2D Gaussian shape.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Elevated perspective looking down-diagonal onto the grid to clearly separate the rows and columns of stems.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant baseline is the m-axis which runs diagonally toward the lower-left, while the n-axis runs diagonally toward the lower-right. (2) This isometric-like layout of the ground plane grid implies a camera azimuth looking from the front-corner (between the negative axes), which is approximately -125 degrees. (3) The vertical stem heights and the grid floor are both clearly visible with foreshortening, suggesting a shallow-to-medium elevation angle of approximately 25 degrees.

interactions.label: Filter Order (N)
interactions.teaches: Controls the size of the binomial filter (N=1 is 2x2, N=2 is 3x3, N=3 is 4x4). Increasing the order makes the discrete bell shape wider and smoother, converging toward a Gaussian.

interactions.label: Show Separability
interactions.teaches: Reveals that this 2D filter is separable: it is created by multiplying a 1D vertical binomial vector by a 1D horizontal binomial vector.
Hovering over individual stems displays their exact binomial coordinate and fractional/integer weight.

demo_steps.title: The 2D Binomial Filter (N=2)
demo_steps.narration: This is the b_{2,2}[n,m] binomial filter. It forms a discrete symmetric bell shape with a central peak of 4 and outer corners of 1. It acts as a smooth, isotropic low-pass filter that avoids the ringing artifacts of a box filter.

demo_steps.title: Separable Construction
demo_steps.narration: Enable separability to see how this 2D filter is composed. The 2D grid of coefficients is the outer product of a 1D row filter [1, 2, 1] and a 1D column filter [1, 2, 1]^T. This makes 2D convolution extremely efficient because it can be computed as two successive 1D convolutions.

demo_steps.title: Minimal 2x2 Filter (N=1)
demo_steps.narration: Lowering the order to N=1 yields a simple 2x2 neighborhood. The coefficients are [1, 1] horizontally and vertically, producing a uniform flat-topped 2D filter. This is the smallest possible binomial blur.

demo_steps.title: Higher Order Blur (N=3)
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the order to N=3 produces a 4x4 grid based on the 1D binomial coefficients [1, 3, 3, 1]. The central coefficients rise to a peak of 9. As N increases, the discrete distribution rapidly approaches a perfect circular 2D Gaussian shape.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Elevated perspective looking down-diagonal onto the grid to clearly separate the rows and columns of stems.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant baseline is the m-axis which runs diagonally toward the lower-left, while the n-axis runs diagonally toward the lower-right. (2) This isometric-like layout of the ground plane grid implies a camera azimuth looking from the front-corner (between the negative axes), which is approximately -125 degrees. (3) The vertical stem heights and the grid floor are both clearly visible with foreshortening, suggesting a shallow-to-medium elevation angle of approximately 25 degrees.

evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer-built interactions are fully implemented and highly robust: (1) A 'Filter Order' slider that dynamically rebuilds the 3D stem grid from N=1 to N=3. (2) A 'Separability' checkbox that toggles an educational 3D projection overlay showing the 1D outer product factors on the back planes with guide lines. Everything is functional and exceptionally well-aligned with the pedagogical goals of teaching 2D binomial filters.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concepts: 2D binomial filters as discrete approximations of Gaussian filters, their separability into 1D horizontal and vertical binomial components, and their DC gain normalization. User-visible claims: (1) Filter order slider (N=1, 2, 3) - accurately updates the 3D grid and binomial coefficient values (e.g., peak of 4 for N=2, peak of 9 for N=3). (2) Separability visual overlay - accurately demonstrates how the 2D coefficients are the outer product of two 1D binomial filters. (3) Tooltip equations - perfectly calculate coordinates, outer products, and normalized fractional gains (e.g., 9/64 for the central stem of N=3). (4) Axis label - The vertical axis label is statically hardcoded as 'b_{2,2}[n,m]' even when the user selects N=1 or N=3, which is technically a mismatch for other orders.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_improvement: Make the vertical axis label dynamic so that it displays 'b_{1,1}[n,m]', 'b_{2,2}[n,m]', or 'b_{3,3}[n,m]' depending on the selected Filter Order (N) slider value, instead of remaining statically hardcoded to 'b_{2,2}'.
